### The Pentagon’s Venezuelan Oil Deal

On January 3, as he announced the seizure of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in a special forces raid, President Donald Trump predicted an oil bonanza for the U.S. "The oil companies are going to go in. They’re going to spend money," he proclaimed. "We’re going to take back the oil that, frankly, we should have taken back a long time ago."

On Friday, Trump followed up on this, announcing on Truth Social an agreement with Venezuela that would significantly increase U.S. government involvement in the country’s oil industry. The Department of Defense would become the dominant shareholder in a new partnership with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), which has pledged to invest up to $100 billion in oil production.

U.S. officials stated that the venture would become the world’s second-largest corporate holder of proven reserves, behind only the majority state-owned Saudi Aramco, which holds roughly 190 billion barrels of crude and condensate.

In a tweet responding to Trump’s post, Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed the deal would lower U.S. gas prices and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela’s economy. Interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez stated the deal would bring endless benefits, including much-needed business investment and tax revenue. The White House called it “the biggest oil deal in world history.”

However, questions remain about the legality of the arrangement for both countries, whether it will produce the claimed 65 million barrels of oil, and whether Rodríguez’s government will endure long enough to see the deal through.

Despite the announcement, neither side has released the text of the agreement, leaving details murky. Reports indicate that the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital would take up to a 35 percent stake in NABEP’s parent company, with rights to buy 20 percent of NABEP’s production at cost and the right of first refusal for the remaining 80 percent.

If realized, this deal would mark the largest ownership stake the executive branch has taken in a private company without express congressional authorization, aside from financial crises or wartime mobilizations. It goes beyond the government’s 15 percent investment in rare-earth miner MP Materials and the 10 percent stake in chipmaker Intel.

Despite Venezuela's vast oil reserves, only a small fraction may be economically viable to extract. The country’s oil infrastructure requires years to develop, and much of it is currently underinvested. NABEP plans to deploy 18 oil rigs by the end of 2027, significantly increasing the number of rigs currently drilling in Venezuela.

There are also legal issues surrounding the deal and the people involved. NABEP is run by Alejandro Betancourt, a Venezuelan tycoon under investigation by Swiss authorities for allegedly laundering funds stolen from his country's state oil company. Despite this, he reportedly received a visa to meet with U.S. officials, and the State Department has pressured Swiss investigators to ease off Betancourt.

Legal experts express skepticism about the deal’s framework, as the Office of Strategic Capital is authorized to lend money for domestic manufacturing and investment in specific covered technologies, but oil is not listed as a covered category.

Moreover, Article 12 of the Venezuelan constitution bars the government from signing over ownership of the country's oil resources, although a recent reform aims to ease private participation in the hydrocarbons sector. The reform caps such arrangements at 25 years, extendable by no more than 15 years. Rodríguez described the deal as a 25-year project, contradicting the White House’s announcement of 100-year concessions.

The U.S. remains committed to a staged democratic transition in Venezuela, with Washington-brokered negotiations leading to some judicial reforms last month, though no election timeline has been set. Experts question whether the oil deal will be viewed positively or as a tool against Rodríguez’s administration.

Rodríguez has pitched the deal as a source of jobs and revenue, but opposition leaders have called it illegitimate, and her government's approval ratings have sharply declined following a slow response to recent disasters.

The situation remains complex as the U.S. navigates its relationship with Venezuela amidst ongoing geopolitical tensions.
